[y=1502 fs=17px] Tokens before components.
[y=1500 fs=17px] Colour, type and spacing first, so everything else has something to stand on.
[y=1570 fs=17px] Only what is used twice.
[y=1568 fs=17px] A component joins the system when two teams need it, not before.
[y=1610 fs=17px] Names a developer can guess.
[y=1608 fs=17px] If you have to look a token up, it has the wrong name.
[y=1649 fs=17px] One owner.
[y=1647 fs=17px] Someone answers for the system every week, or nobody does.
[y=1699 fs=31.68px] A design system is a product. Its users are your own team.
[y=1859 fs=32px] What it took
[y=1936 fs=17px] Six months, one designer and one engineer part-time. The button count went from 31 to four, and new screens now take days instead of weeks.

[y=1245 fs=32px] Three questions
[y=1321 fs=17px] Before anything moves on screen, I ask three things:
[y=1351 fs=17px] What changed, and does the person need to notice?
[y=1390 fs=17px] Where did it come from, and where is it going?
[y=1429 fs=17px] Would it be clearer if it did not move at all?
[y=1519 fs=32px] Motion as explanation
[y=1595 fs=17px] Good motion answers a question the person was about to ask: where did that panel go, what did I just delete, is it still loading. Motion that answers nothing is decoration, and decoration gets tiring by the third visit.
[y=1706 fs=31.68px] If you can't say why it moves, it shouldn't.
[y=1828 fs=32px] Keep it short
[y=1904 fs=17px] Most interface motion should finish in under 300 milliseconds. Anything longer makes people wait for the interface instead of the other way round.

[y=1268 fs=32px] Why not by the day
[y=1344 fs=17px] Day rates reward slow work and punish clear thinking. Clients also hate them, because the number they care about — the total — is the one nobody can tell them.
[y=1464 fs=32px] Fixed scope, fixed price
[y=1540 fs=17px] After a first call I write a one-page proposal: what we will make, what we will not, how long it takes and what it costs. If the scope changes, the price changes, in writing, before the work.
[y=1598 fs=17px] A one-week sprint to start, priced on its own
[y=1638 fs=17px] Then a fixed quote for the build
[y=1677 fs=17px] Payment in three parts, the last one on launch
[y=1767 fs=32px] Why not by the screen
[y=1843 fs=17px] Screens are a bad unit. A settings page and an onboarding flow are both 'one screen' and differ by weeks of work.
[y=1925 fs=31.68px] Price the result, not the hours and not the pixels.

[y=1245 fs=32px] The debate
[y=1321 fs=17px] A team I worked with had argued for six weeks about how a new search should work. Three slide decks, two workshops, no decision.
[y=1441 fs=32px] 200 lines
[y=1517 fs=17px] I built a rough prototype in an afternoon: real data, real typing, no styling. We put it in front of five customers the next morning.
[y=1575 fs=17px] Two of the three ideas died in the first ten minutes
[y=1615 fs=17px] The third needed one change nobody had predicted
[y=1654 fs=17px] The decision took one meeting
[y=1706 fs=31.68px] A prototype is the cheapest way to have the argument you were going to have anyway.
[y=1866 fs=32px] When to do it
[y=1943 fs=17px] Whenever a discussion is about how something behaves rather than how it looks. Slides are good at the second and useless at the first.
